title: GPU pool slab pricing + idle-sink analysis
summary: Working spreadsheet and narrative exploring an alternative slab-based pricing construct for reserved GPU pools and an accompanying "idle-sink" credit mechanism to reduce churn from short-term underutilization. Focus is modeling amortization, cross-customer pooling, and the marginal economics of burst vs soft-reserve buckets.
key-assumptions: Average committed GPU spec: A100-80GB equivalent
Baseline on-prem cost per GPU (amortized infra + power): $2.40/hour
Hosted operating markup target: 2.1x of infra costs for Dedicated baseline
Commit term considered: 12-month default, 3 and 24 month variants modeled
Expected baseline utilization (historical): 47% across committed pools
Burst capacity premium: 1.8x marginal cost for on-demand/spot attachments
Idle-sink mechanism: credits issued proportional to minutes of idle below 40% per pool per month
scenario-highlights: Slab tiers (small/medium/large pools) smooth unit price for customers with sustained usage: largest slab yields ~17% lower $/GPU-hour compared to tiny slab under identical amortization assumptions.
Idle-sink credits reduce bilateral churn: simulation shows customers with seasonal dips keep contracts 28% longer when credits offset 60% of monthly underutilization delta.
Cross-customer pooling (internal multiplex) increases realized utilization by 9-14% versus isolated pools for same commit size in heterogeneous workloads.
Bursting into a shared spot buffer is cost-effective up to 22% burst mix; beyond that, recommend reclassifying to a larger committed slab.
Amortization window sensitivity: extending to 24 months lowers unit cost by ~11% but increases revenue risk if churn spikes; short 3-month terms blow up per-hour price by >40%.
recommended-pricing-constructs: Slab-based commits: price per GPU-hour steps down at defined pool sizes (1-8, 9-32, 33+). Offer explicit pool-level SLA tiers tied to slab size.

Idle-sink credit: issue monthly credits when pool utilization < idle_threshold (default 40%). Credit = (idle_delta_hours * slab_hourly_rate * credit_conversion_rate). Credits redeemable against next invoice or to extend burst budget.
Soft-reserve buffer: a small portion of each slab (5-10% capacity) allocated for predictable short bursts at lower premium than on-demand, reducing need to escalate to expensive on-demand instances.
Inter-pool swap credits: allow limited cross-commit swap windows each quarter, with a swap fee and potential re-amortization option for long-term rebalancing.
Progressive amortization schedule: default 12-month amortization, optional 24-month for enterprise with discount floors and minimum utilization covenants to protect revenue.
Clear revert policy: if average utilization stays <25% for two consecutive quarters, trigger auto-conversion to pay-as-you-go at predefined fallback rates.
idle-sink-mechanics-summary: Idle-sink is a customer-facing credit ledger line that reduces the short-term pain of seasonality. It is not refunded cash; it offsets future invoices or is consumed to buy burst credits. Implementation requires monthly utilization reporting per pool, a validation window, and a capped credit balance (suggested 1x monthly committed spend).
amortization-math-note: Amortized cost per GPU-hour = (total infra capex + expected maintenance over term) / (committed_gpus * 24 * 30 * term_months * expected_realized_utilization). Ensure to include expected reclaim windows in denominator for more conservative public offering.

Pricing: draft slab threshold pricing table for legal review and produce 3 sample quotes across ARR bands.
SRE: prototype soft-reserve buffer orchestration in staging; measure tail-latency effects under 20% and 40% burst mixes.
Product: prepare a short pilot offer for 5 existing mid-market customers that maps current commits into slab proposals and track churn/uptake over 90 days.

notes-to-exec: This sheet is an exploratory hybrid: the slab + idle-sink combo aims to balance predictable revenue with a pragmatic customer experience for teams that cannot sustain consistent utilization. The pilot should be priced conservatively; the primary risk is revenue erosion if we underprice slabs for customers who migrate to higher burst mixes. Recommend limited pilot, close monitoring, and tying broader rollout to telemetry-backed utilization improvements (>=5% realized uplift) and legal signoff on credit mechanics.
